stem: Which entry transfers the **cost** of an asset sold to the disposal account?

options.content: Debit disposal; credit the asset account
options.rationale: Correct: the asset account is cleared of the cost.

options.content: Debit the asset account; credit disposal
options.rationale: This is the reverse entry.

options.content: Debit disposal; credit provision for depreciation
options.rationale: Depreciation is transferred the other way: debit provision, credit disposal.

options.content: Debit bank; credit the asset account
options.rationale: Proceeds are credited to the disposal account, not the asset account.

explanation: Step 1 of a disposal: debit disposal, credit the asset account with the cost.

stem: On the disposal account, which side records the accumulated depreciation on the asset sold?

options.rationale: Correct: debit provision for depreciation, credit disposal.
The cost is on the debit side; depreciation reduces it from the credit side.

options.content: It is not recorded in the disposal account
options.rationale: It must be transferred to find the net book value.

options.content: Either side, depending on whether there is a profit
options.rationale: The side is fixed; only the balancing figure depends on profit or loss.

explanation: Cost on the debit side, less depreciation and proceeds on the credit side; the difference is the profit or loss.

stem: A computer system cost US\$13,500. Accumulated depreciation at the date of sale was US\$8,640. It was sold for US\$5,400. What is the result on disposal?

options.rationale: Proceeds are above net book value, so it is a profit.
This compares proceeds with cost and ignores depreciation.
This compares proceeds with the depreciation, not the net book value.

stem: Where is a **loss** on disposal of a non-current asset shown?

options.content: Added to gross profit as other income
options.rationale: That is where a profit on disposal goes.

options.content: As an expense in the income statement
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Deducted from capital in the statement of financial position
options.rationale: It reaches capital only through the profit for the year.
Nothing is owed.

explanation: A loss on disposal is an expense; a profit on disposal is other income.

stem: Rudo trades in an old delivery bike for a new one costing US\$4,800. The dealer allows US\$1,150 for the old bike and Rudo pays the balance by bank transfer. At what amount is the **new** bike debited to the motorcycles account in total?

options.rationale: This is only the cash paid.
This is the allowance for the old bike.
Correct: allowance 1,150 + cash 3,650 = full cost.
The allowance is part of the price, not an extra cost.

explanation: Debit motorcycles 1,150 (credit disposal) and 3,650 (credit bank): total 4,800.
hints: The new asset is recorded at its full cost.

stem: A business makes a large profit on disposal of a machine. What does this most likely show?

options.content: The machine was bought at too low a price
options.rationale: The purchase price does not explain the gap between proceeds and net book value.

options.content: The business's trading activities were very profitable
options.rationale: Disposal profit is not trading profit.

options.content: The machine should not have been depreciated at all
options.rationale: All machines wear out; the rate was probably too high.

options.content: Too much depreciation was charged on the machine in earlier years
options.rationale: Correct: the net book value had fallen below what the machine was worth.

explanation: A profit on disposal corrects over-depreciation in earlier years; a loss corrects under-depreciation.
hints: Profit on disposal = proceeds − net book value.

stem: A van bought for US\$20,000 was depreciated at 25% per annum on the reducing balance for two full years and then sold for US\$10,600. What was the result on disposal?

options.rationale: This uses straight-line depreciation (25% of cost each year).
Correct: NBV 11,250, proceeds 10,600.
This ignores depreciation.
Proceeds are below net book value: a loss.

hints: Work out the net book value year by year.

stem: After a disposal has been recorded, the disposal account has no balance to carry forward.
explanation: True. The balancing figure (profit or loss) is transferred to the income statement, closing the account.

stem: In a part-exchange, the trade-in allowance for the old asset is treated as its sale proceeds.
explanation: True. Debit the asset account (new asset) and credit the disposal account with the allowance.

stem: Gift sells a delivery van. Match each disposal-account entry with its double entry.

left.content: Depreciation on the van to date

right.content: Dr Provision for depreciation, Cr Disposal

explanation: Cost in, depreciation and proceeds out; the balancing figure goes to the income statement.

payload.template: Profit or loss on disposal = proceeds − {{blank:a}}. A {{blank:b}} on disposal is a debit balancing figure on the disposal account.

explanation: When proceeds exceed net book value the credits exceed the debits, so the profit is the debit balancing figure.

stem: Farai bought a cold-room on 1 January 2021 for US\$38,400. It is depreciated at 12.5% per annum on cost, with a full year's charge in the year of purchase and none in the year of sale. He sold it on 1 March 2025 for US\$19,750. Calculate the profit on disposal.
explanation: Depreciation 12.5% × 38,400 = 4,800 a year for 4 years = 19,200. NBV 38,400 − 19,200 = 19,200. Profit 19,750 − 19,200 = 550. Comparing proceeds with cost gives 18,650; charging five years (including 2025) gives 5,350.
workedSolution: 1. Depreciation 12.5% × 38,400 = 4,800 a year for 4 years = 19,200. NBV 38,400 − 19,200 = 19,200. Profit 19,750 − 19,200 = 550. Comparing proceeds with cost gives 18,650; charging five years (including 2025) gives 5,350.
hints: Net book value = cost − accumulated depreciation.

stem: Chipo bought a photocopier for her stationery shop on 1 August 2023 for US\$7,200 plus installation of US\$2,400. Depreciation is 20% per annum on cost, on a monthly basis. She sold the photocopier on 31 May 2025 for US\$5,700. Calculate the loss on disposal.
explanation: Cost 7,200 + 2,400 = 9,600. Annual depreciation 20% × 9,600 = 1,920. Months owned: 5 (2023) + 12 (2024) + 5 (2025) = 22, so depreciation 1,920 × 22/12 = 3,520. NBV 9,600 − 3,520 = 6,080. Loss 6,080 − 5,700 = 380. Charging two full years gives a loss of 60.
workedSolution: 1. Cost 7,200 + 2,400 = 9,600. Annual depreciation 20% × 9,600 = 1,920. Months owned: 5 (2023) + 12 (2024) + 5 (2025) = 22, so depreciation 1,920 × 22/12 = 3,520. NBV 9,600 − 3,520 = 6,080. Loss 6,080 − 5,700 = 380. Charging two full years gives a loss of 60.
hints: Installation is part of the cost.
Count the months owned: August 2023 to May 2025.

stem: Explain why a profit on the disposal of a non-current asset is not part of the business's trading profit.

points.description: It does not arise from buying and selling goods / normal trading activities
It is an adjustment for over-depreciation in earlier years, so it is shown as other income below gross profit

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Selling a used asset is not the business's trade; the profit only shows that earlier depreciation was too high, so it is added as other income, not included in gross profit.
